doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: Creative ambitions and the jazz business
title: Harmolodics and the lack of musical training among critics
summary: Asked about Ornette Coleman, he says critics lack musical backgrounds and his own harmonic work has gone unnoticed for ten years.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: It reminds me of Ornette Coleman’s—
The Harmolodic but I’m not sure I understand it.

Well see that’s the thing. See that’s something that again bothers me, and to me shows a deficiency of the jazz criticism and the fact that I mean like some of the jazz critics I have good relationships with, some I would even, one or two I would even consider kind of friends. But speaking in general terms they usually don’t have a serious musical

background, which that doesn’t invalidate all their opinions, but I think sometimes it puts them at a disadvantage. And the thing is, take for instance Ornette Coleman. And I have great respect for him, especially the stuff he did with Don Cherry, a lot of that stuff I think is great. And he really opened up things, and an incredibly important figure. But for instance like “Harmolodic” is this term that every musician knows but nobody knows what it is. And I’ll say I’m not sure that Ornette Coleman, if it is a specific thing. I mean he’s got an approach, I don’t mean to deny that, but to say like you can break it down the way you can like a Baroque contrapuntal technique or something, I don’t think it’s that specific. Well the stuff that I’ve worked on it is very specific. It does really relate music to harmony. I’m not saying that it’s the greatest thing since sliced bread, but I’m saying that it does deserve a little bit of attention and I’ll tell you, and I’ve been doing it live in New York, I’ve been doing it for ten years. It’s been like pulling teeth.
